html:
The British Agricultural Revolution was the large rise in farm output in Britain between the late 1600s and the mid 1800s. Fewer farmers grew more food, which fed a growing population and freed workers for the towns and factories of the Industrial Revolution.

It was not one invention but many changes adding up over generations:

  • New crop rotations. The Norfolk four course system rotated wheat, turnips, barley and clover. Turnips fed animals over winter and clover put nitrogen back into the soil, so land no longer had to lie fallow.
  • Enclosure: open fields and common land were fenced into private farms, often by Acts of Parliament. Farmers could then try new methods, but many poor villagers lost their grazing rights.
  • Selective breeding of sheep and cattle, made famous by Robert Bakewell.
  • Better ploughs, drainage and, later, Jethro Tull's seed drill and new fertilisers.
  • New crops from the Americas, above all the potato.

Output grew faster than population for about a century before 1770. England could feed a population that roughly tripled between 1700 and 1850, though from the 1840s it relied more and more on imports.

The change also reshaped society. Land became concentrated in large estates rented to commercial farmers, who hired labourers. Some historians stress the losers of enclosure; others stress how much the extra food mattered. The extra food also kept the market towns busy and fed London. Many of the ideas came from the Low Countries, but Britain applied them on a large scale.
